en: Salutations to Śrī Gaṇeśa. Salutations to Śrī Dattātreya.
The sages said:
"O Vedavyāsa, how may the fulfillment of one's intentions be achieved in the Kali age?"
What is declared to be the means for achieving dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa? || 1 ||
Vyāsa said:
"Listen, all you sages, to the means for accomplishing one's resolve, which bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation by the mere act of reciting it once. (2)
On the peak of Gauri on Mount Himavat, adorned with wish-fulfilling trees,
he stood in the center of a blazing pavilion made of divine great jewels and gold.
Pārvatī spoke to Śaṅkara, the Supreme Lord, who was seated upon a jeweled lion-throne, serene, with a lotus-face marked by a gentle smile.
The Śrī Devī said: O God of gods, Mahādeva, Śaṅkara, benefactor of the world! [Tell me of] all the networks of mantras and the entire collection of yantras.
Indeed, many networks of tantras have been heard by me from you;
now I especially desire to see the surface of the earth.
Having heard what was thus spoken by Pārvatī, the Supreme Lord, stroking her with his hand out of delight, replied to Pārvatī.
"Now you must go with me, mounted upon the bull.
Having spoken thus, Śaṅkara, together with Pārvatī, mounted the bull.
Displaying the various wonders of Gaurī, he traveled across the earth to behold it,
at times reaching the edge of the Vindhya mountains in a vast and most inaccessible forest.
There, he saw a Bhilla approaching with an axe to speak [to him],
like a great tiger being provoked and covered with claws and fangs.
Possessing exceedingly wonderful conduct and endowed with a vajra-body, he abides in total bliss, effortless and without exertion. || 11 ||
Seeing this wonder— that the tiger fled in fear behind a fleeing deer— Pārvatī spoke to Śaṅkara.
Śrī Pārvatī said:
"What wonder! What wonder! O Śambhu, look ahead!
Being thus addressed, Śambhu, the knower of the Purāṇas, looked and then spoke.
Śrī Śaṅkara said:
O Gaurī, I shall tell you of a wonder that is beyond the reach of speech and mind;
it has never been seen by us before, and there is nothing like it anywhere.
I shall explain it correctly and in brief; listen, O Pārvatī!
This Bhilla named Dūraśravas is supremely righteous.
Having gone daily to the forest, he would laboriously gather sacrificial fuel, *kuśa* grass, flowers, tubers, roots, fruits, and other such items.
O beloved, he formerly gave to the lords of sages yet did not desire anything in return;
even they, who are all silent, show compassion toward him.
While dwelling in his own hermitage, the great yogi Dalādana once remembered the Siddha Dattātreya, who was clad only in the directions.
If Dattātreya were to go to those who remember him in order to test their history,
then at that very moment, that lord of yogis, Dattātreya, would also arise.
Seeing him, the great sage Dalādana, filled with wonder and joy,
honored Dattātreya as he sat before him and spoke to him.
"O great sage Dattātreya, I have been summoned by Māyā and have arrived;
this is to test the popular saying that 'you go wherever you are thought of. (21)
"Today you have been remembered by me; forgive my transgression.
Dattātreya said to the sage, "Such is my very nature."
Whether with lack of devotion or with great devotion, whoever remembers me with undivided mind—
at that moment, having approached him, I grant whatever he desires.
Dattātreya said to the sage Dalādana, the lord of munis:
"Choose whatever you desire, since I have been reached by you through your remembrance."
The sage said to Dattātreya: "I shall not say anything at all;
O bull among sages, give me that which resides within your mind."
Śrī Dattātreya said:
"I possess the Vajra-kavaca; take it," he said to the sage.
To Dalādana-muni, who accepted this saying "It is true," the sage [bestowed it].
He spoke his own Vajra-armor, preceded by the seers and the meters, including the ritual placement (*nyāsa*), the meditation (*dhyāna*), the fruit, and the purpose therein in their entirety. (27)
Of this *Śrī-Dattātreya-Vajrakavaca-Stotra-Mantra*:
the Seer (*ṛṣi*) is Mahārudra in the form of Kirāta; the Metre (*chandaḥ*) is Anuṣṭubh;
the Deity (*devatā*) is Śrī-Dattātreya; the Seed-syllable (*bīja*) is *drāṃ*; the Power (*śakti*) is *āṃ*.
*Krauṃ* is the *kīlaka*. *Oṃ ātmane namaḥ*. *Oṃ drīṃ manase namaḥ*.
*Oṃ āṃ drīṃ śrīṃ sauḥ oṃ klāṃ klīṃ klūṃ klaiṃ klauṃ klaḥ*.
This is the application (*viniyoga*) for the purpose of attaining the grace of Śrī Dattātreya during the recitation (*japa*).
Oṃ drāṃ, homage to the two thumbs. Oṃ drīṃ, homage to the two index fingers.
Oṃ drūṃ, homage to the two middle fingers.
Oṃ draiṃ, salutation to the two ring fingers. Oṃ drauṃ, salutation to the two little fingers. Oṃ draḥ, salutation to the palms and backs of the hands.
Thus is the placement [of mantras] on the heart and other parts.
With "oṃ bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ oṃ," there is the binding of the directions. Now, the meditation:
Salutations to Dattātreya, the Supreme Self, the moon among the lords of yogis, whose form is existence, consciousness, and bliss, and who is the root of the sprout and the bulb of the world-tree.
Sometimes a yogi, sometimes an enjoyer, and sometimes naked like a ghost—
Dattātreya is Hari himself, the bestower of both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
Bathing in the city of Vārāṇasī, devoted to the recitation of mantras at Kolhāpura,
subsisting on alms in the city of Māhurī, he slept upon the Sahya mountains as a naked ascetic.
Having a form like sapphire and a luster equal to the moon's radiance,
with a brilliance resembling lapis lazuli, he wore a few strands of matted hair that were slightly swaying.
His eyes were glossy and white with extremely dark pupils;
his eyebrows, chest, and beard were marked with blue, and his face resembled the moon.
His laughter has conquered the frost; his neck has surpassed the conch shell;
he has muscular shoulders and long arms; and his hands have bested the young sprouts.
He had a broad and full chest, copper-colored palms, and a leaf-like belly;
he was graceful with wide hips and expansive buttocks.
His thighs were like the trunks of plantain trees, his knees were followed by shapely calves,
his ankles were hidden, and the tops of his feet shone with the curvature of a tortoise shell.
With lips as lovely as red lotuses,
the yogi, clad in a garment of skin, goes to the minds of those who remember him at every moment.
Delighting in the instruction of knowledge, consecrated for the removal of calamities,
seated upon a perfected posture, with body straight and face smiling;
With his left hand he displays the gesture of granting boons (varada) and with his right the gesture of fearlessness (abhayakara);
in some places he is observed accompanied by children, madmen, and female goblins (piśācīs).
He is the renouncer, the enjoyer, the great yogi, eternally blissful, and stainless;
he possesses all forms, is the giver of all, omnipresent, and the granter of all desires.
With all his limbs smeared with ashes, he is the destroyer of great sins;
he bestows enjoyment and grants liberation, being liberated while living—of this there is no doubt.
Having meditated thus with an undistracted mind, one should recite my vajra-armor;
seeing me everywhere, he shall move about together with me.
Clad in the directions as his garment, smeared with fragrant ashes, bearing the discus, trident, hand-drum, and mace as weapons,
seated upon a lotus throne, and worshipped by the lords of yogis and sages— by constantly remembering the name "Datta," [one attains him].
Oṃ! May Dattātreya, who resides upon a thousand lotuses, protect my head;
may Anasūyā, who dwells in the center of the lunar disc, protect my forehead. (28)

May the mind-born Kūrca protect [me]; may Haṃ Kṣaṃ, born from the double-petaled lotus, protect me; may the one whose form is light protect my eyes, and may the one whose essence is sound protect my ears.
May He whose essence is fragrance protect the nose; may He whose essence is taste protect the mouth;
may He whose essence is the Vedas protect the tongue; and may He who is the embodiment of righteousness protect the teeth and lips.

May the Lord who dwells on the cheeks protect me; may He, the knower of all, protect me entirely. May the Self of the vowels, situated upon the sixteen-petalled lotus, as my own Self, protect my throat.
May the younger brother of Candra protect my shoulders; may the source of the Kṛta age and others protect my arms;
may the conqueror of enemies protect my collarbones; and may Hari protect the region of my chest.
May he who resides in the twelve-petaled lotus from Ka to Tha, whose nature is that of the vital breath (marut), the Lord of the Lords of Yogins, protect my heart as he dwells within the heart. 33.
May Hari, who dwells at the side, protect [me]; he is remembered as standing at the side.
May the ocean of compassion, who knows the yoga of Haṭha and other yogas, protect my belly. 34.
May the one whose nature is fire, abiding in the ten-petalled lotus of the navel region—beginning with the letter *ḍa* and ending with the letter *pha*—protect the navel. (35)
May the yogi, whose nature is the essence of fire, protect the maṇipūra;
may he, who is the soul of Vāsudeva residing in the Brahmāṇḍa at the waist, protect the waist.
May the Yogin, who consists of the principle of water, who awakens the six-petaled lotus beginning with the letter *va* and ending with the letter *la*, protect my Svādhiṣṭhāna. (37)
May Siddheśvara, seated upon the Siddhāsana, protect my thighs—he who is the knower of the four-petalled lotus beginning with *va* and ending with *sa*. (38)
May He who restrains His own vigor protect the *mūlādhāra* in the form of the earth;
and may He, with His lotus-like hands placed upon His knees, protect [my] back from all sides. (39)
May the Lord of the shaken (Avadhūteśvara) protect the shanks; may the Purifier of Holy Places (Tīrthapāvana) protect the feet;
may the Soul of All (Sarvātmā) protect the entire body; and may Keśava protect the hairs of the body. 40.
May he who wears skin protect my skin; may he who is fond of devotion protect my blood;
may he who creates flesh protect my flesh; may he whose essence is marrow protect my marrow. || 41 ||
May the Firm-minded protect the bones; may the Creator preserve my intellect;
may the Bringer of Happiness protect the semen; and may He of Steadfast Form protect the mind. || 42 ||
May He whose nature is Hṛṣīkeśa protect the mind, intellect, and ego;
may the Lord protect the organs of action, and may the Unborn protect the organs of knowledge.
May the best of kinsmen protect his kin from enemies; may the conqueror of foes protect [us] from enemies; and may Śaṅkara protect our homes, gardens, wealth, fields, sons, and so forth. 44.
May He who knows the primordial nature protect his wife; may the wielder of the Śārṅga bow protect his cattle and other possessions;
may He who knows the Pradhāna protect his vital breaths; and may the Sun-god protect his food and other sustenance.
May He whose nature is the Moon protect me with bliss; may the Destroyer of Cities protect me from suffering;
may the Lord of Beasts protect my followers; and may the Lord of Beings protect my prosperity. (46)
May the Dispeller of Poison protect me in the east; may He whose nature is the Sacrifice protect me in the southeast;
may He whose nature is Dharma protect me in the south; and may the Remover of All Enemies protect me in the southwest.
May Varāha protect in the western quarter; may the Giver of Breath protect in the northwestern quarter;
may the Giver of Wealth protect in the northern quarter; and may the Great Preceptor protect in the northeastern quarter. (48)
May the Great Siddha protect [me] above; may the wearer of matted locks protect below;
and may the Lord of Sages, Ādimuni, protect that place which is devoid of protection. 49.
Whoever should read or even hear this Vajra Armor of mine shall possess a vajra-body and live for a long time; thus I, Dattātreya, have declared.
A renouncer, an enjoyer, a great yogi, and one freed from pleasure and pain—he whose resolve is perfected in all things stands today as one liberated while living. (52)
Having spoken thus, the sky-clad yogi Dattātreya vanished;
and Dalādana, having chanted that [mantra], remains liberated while living.
At that time, a Bhilla named Dūraśrava,
merely by hearing [the name] once, became Vajrāṅga upon hearing it.
Having heard this entire Vajrakavaca from the mouth of Śambhu, Pārvatī spoke again to the yogin Dattātreya.
Pārvatī said:
Tell me in detail this greatness of the armor (kavaca):
where, by whom, and when is it to be recited; what is to be recited, and how, and in what manner?
Śambhu spoke all that which had been addressed with humility by Pārvatī.
Śrī Śiva said:
"Listen, O Pārvatī; I shall speak with a composed and undisturbed mind. (57)
This alone is the supreme refuge for dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa;
it bestows all sovereignty, including elephants, horses, chariots, and infantry.
For that is indeed the supreme means for satisfying all—sons, friends, wives, and others—and it is the ultimate treasury of the sciences such as the Vedas and the Shastras. (59)
It bestows proficiency in the science of music, literature, and the composition of fine poetry; it grants intelligence, knowledge, memory, wisdom, and mental acumen. || 60 ||
It brings satisfaction to all, wards off all suffering, swiftly destroys enemies, and increases fame and renown. (61)
There are eight types of major diseases, thirteen types of *sannipāta* disorders, ninety-six eye diseases, and twenty urinary disorders. (62)
There are eighteen types of skin diseases (kuṣṭha), eight kinds of abdominal tumors (gulma), eighty diseases of wind (vāta), and forty of bile (pitta). 63.

The twenty diseases caused by phlegm, as well as wasting diseases, quartan fevers, and so forth; and those produced by spells, mechanical devices, and evil yogas, as well as those fashioned through ritual manuals (kalpas) and tantras. (64)

Those arising from grahas such as Brahmarākṣasas, Vetālas, and Kūṣmāṇḍas; those born of association; those residing in particular places and times; and those originating from the three types of suffering (tāpa). || 65 ||
All diseases arising from the nine planets and born of great sins are certainly destroyed by reciting [this] one thousand times. (66)
By reciting it ten thousand times, a barren woman shall become possessed of sons; by reciting it twenty thousand times, one shall indeed conquer untimely death.
From three times ten thousand [repetitions], the power of moving through the sky (khecaratva) arises;
from one thousand up to ten thousand, one shall accomplish all undertakings.
By reciting it one hundred thousand times, the accomplishment of the task will surely come to pass; of this there is no doubt.
Standing at the roots of a poison tree, facing the south, [one should perform the rite]. (69)
One who desires prosperity should recite [the mantra] at the root of an Udumbara tree; within a single month, he renders his enemy one whose senses are impaired. 70.
One desiring prosperity should [meditate] at the foot of a banyan tree; one desiring fortune at the foot of a tamarind tree for rites of pacification;
one desiring vital energy at the foot of an aśvattha tree; and those desiring women at the foot of a mango tree. (71)
One seeking knowledge should worship at the root of a *tulasī* plant; those seeking a son, in the inner sanctum (*garbhagṛha*);
those seeking wealth, in a fertile field; and those desiring cattle, in a cow-pen.
In a temple, at that time, when all desires are revealed by all [the deities], he who stands in water reaching up to his navel and gazes at the sun while reciting [the mantra]... || 73 ||
In battle or in a debate on the scriptures, victory shall come by the thousand for one who recites this armor-mantra at night while standing in water up to the neck. || 74 ||
It wards off the fever of afflictions such as fever, epilepsy, leprosy, and the like;
wherever and whatever may be present, that which is stable and clear is brought to cessation.
"Therefore, one must indeed recite [the mantra] there; from that, success will surely come.
Having spoken thus to Gaurī, Śiva [revealed] this most auspicious secret. (76)
Whoever recites this Vajrakavaca shall become equal to Dattātreya;
thus was it spoken by Śiva to the daughter of Himavat.
To the sage Dalāda, the son of Atri, he previously gave this Vajrakavaca;
whoever in this world recites it becomes like a gift bestowed, and as an excellent yogi, he wanders with long life. (78)
Thus ends the Śrī Dattātreyavajrakavaca Stotra, within the Himavat-khaṇḍa of the Śrī Rudrayāmala, in the dialogue between Umā and Maheśvara.
